d: Unpleasantly and excessively suave or ingratiating in manner or speech
ety: From Late Middle English unctuous [and other forms], borrowed from Medieval Latin ūnctuōsus (“greasy, oily, unctuous”), from Latin ūnctum (“ointment; rich banquet; rich savoury dish”) + -ōsus (suffix meaning ‘full of; overly’ forming adjectives from nouns). Ūnctum is a noun use of the perfect passive participle of unguō (“to anoint; to smear with oil, to grease or oil”), from Proto-Indo-European *
s: General Peckem roused himself after a moment with an unctuous and benignant smile.

d: The 3rd syllable of a word counting back from the end
ety: From ante- + penultimate, modelled on Latin antepaenultima/antepēnultima (syllaba) (“last syllable but two in a word”), from the feminine of antepaenultimus/antepēnultimus (“antepenultimate”).
s: The words animal, citizen, comedy, and antepenultimate are stressed on the antepenultimate.

d: Lack of honesty; acts of lying or cheating or stealing
ety: From knave + -ery.
s: O, Hang 'em—no—wine does but draw forth a man's natural qualities; and to make them drink would only be to whet their Knavery.

d: A member of a European military unit formerly composed of heavily armed cavalrymen
ety: The noun is borrowed from French dragon (“dragon (mythological creature); type of cavalry soldier, dragoon”) (originally referring to a soldier armed with the firearm of the same name (noun sense 1.1)), ultimately from Latin dracō (“dragon; kind of serpent or snake”), from Ancient Greek δρᾰ́κων (drắkōn, “dragon; serpent”), possibly from δέρκομαι (dérkomai, “to see, see clearly (in the sense of som
s: The French persecution more inhuman than ever. The Protestants in Savoy successfully resist the French dragoons sent to murder them.

d: Admit openly and bluntly; make no bones about
ety: From Old French avouchier, from Latin advocāre. Doublet of advocate, advoke, and avow.
s: If this which he avouches does appear, There is nor flying hence nor tarrying here.

d: Brilliant and showy technical skill
ety: From Italian bravura (“skill”), from bravo (“good, skilful”). Compare bravado.
s: In a final bravura the ballerina appeared to be floating in water.

d: Destroy completely, as if down to the roots
ety: The verb is first attested in 1538, the adjective in 1541; borrowed from Latin exstirpātus perfect passive participle of exstirpō (“to uproot”), from ex- (“out of”) + stirps (“the lower part of the trunk of a tree, including the roots; the stem, stalk”) + -ō (verb-forming suffix) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (adjective-forming suffix)). Doublet of extirp. Common participial usage of th
s: The simple object was to expel the natives, and to extirpate the Catholic religion.

d: An insufficient quantity or number
ety: From Middle English paucete, paucite, paucyte, partly from Middle French paucité and partly from its etymon, Latin paucitās (“a small number, fewness, scarcity”), from paucus (“few, little”). Related to few.
s: Here is where the paucity of our language is made manifest.

d: A metal urn with a spigot at the base; used in Russia to boil water for tea
ety: From Russian самова́р (samovár, “self-boiler”); from само́ (samó, “self”) + вари́ть (varítʹ, “boil, cook”).
s: Come on now with the samovar ─ and make haste sorting the letter-bag.

d: (of animals or plants) having stiff coarse hairs or bristles
ety: From Latin hispidus (“rough, hairy, bristly”).
s: The hispid hare inhabits forested areas.

d: Not growing or changing; without force or vitality
ety: From Latin moribundus (“dying”).
s: These moribund shapes were free as air—and nearly as thin.

d: An expression introduced into one language by translating it from another language
ety: From French calque (“calque”, literally “copy, tracing”), from calquer (“to copy, trace”) (whence also calk), itself borrowed from Italian calcare, from Latin calcāre (“to tread”). Doublet of calcate and calcation.
s: One of the primary benefits of calque is its ability to enhance cross-cultural communication.

d: A state of extreme poverty or destitution
ety: From Late Middle English penuri, penurie (“destitution, need, poverty; dearth, lack, scarcity”), borrowed from Latin pēnūria (“need, scarcity, want”) + Middle English -i, -ie (suffix forming abstract and collective nouns); further etymology uncertain, possibly related to paene (“almost, nearly; barely, hardly, scarcely”, adverb), possibly from Proto-Indo-European *peh₁- (“to hate; to hurt”).
s: In all labour there is profit: but the talke of the lippes tendeth onely to penury.

d: A chamber that is used as a grave
ety: From Middle English sepulchre, sepulcre, sepulker, from late Old English sepulcer, Old French sepulchre, sepulcre, and their etymon Latin sepulchrum, sepulcrum (“grave, burial place”).
s: I parked Bertha in a convenient cab rank and raced into the smoked glass sepulchre that is Hanover airport.

d: Someone who sleeps in any convenient place
ety: From doss + -er.
s: Illustrating the strength of feeling, some said Dorries was “never here and is as useful as a chocolate teapot”, while “Dosser Dorries” posters appeared in the area.

d: A sudden jarring impact
ety: The verb is derived from Late Middle English *jouncen (“to jolt violently”) (evidenced by jouncinge (“violent jolting movement”)); further etymology unknown, possibly imitative. The noun is probably derived from the verb as it is attested later.
s: When the drive axles have inner and outer joints, rear wheel camber change is minimized during wheel jounce and rebound.

d: An archaic word originally meaning ‘in truth’ but now usually used to express disbelief
ety: From Middle English forsothe, forsoþe, for sothe, from Old English for sōþ (“truly, for certain, forsooth”), equivalent to for (“for, by”) + sooth (“truth”).
s: A fit man, forsooth, to governe a realme!

d: The property of being close together
ety: From propinqu(ent) + -ity, from Middle English propinquite, from Middle French propinquité or Latin propinquitās, from propinquus (“neighbouring”) (from prop(e) (“near”) + (h)inc (“hence”) + -uus).
s: Propinquity and corruption don't always go side by side.

d: A stupid person; these words are used to express a low opinion of someone’s intelligence
ety: From logger (“(dialectal) heavy wooden block secured to a horse's leg to prevent it from straying”) + head. Logger was apparently coined because its sound connotes a clumsy, heavy object; compare log (“trunk of a dead tree; bulky piece of wood”).
s: Loggerheads, from the resemblance of its knobbed involucres to a weapon so called, consisting of a ball of iron at the end of a stick, the knapweed, the Clobbewed of old MSS. Centaurea nigra, L.

d: A tangible symbol signifying approval or distinction
ety: First use appears c. 1591 in the publications of Thomas Lodge, borrowed from French accolade, from Occitan acolada (“an embrace”), from acolar (“to embrace”), from Italian accollato, via Vulgar Latin *accollō (“to hug around the neck”), from Latin ad- + collum (“neck”) (English collar) + -āta.
s: The scientist received the highest accolade in her field for the groundbreaking discovery.

d: Young and inexperienced
ety: From Middle English calwe (“(adjective) bald; (noun) bald person”), from Old English calu, caluw (“without hair, bald, callow”), from Proto-West Germanic *kalu, from Proto-Germanic *kalwaz (“bald; bare, naked”), and then either: * from Proto-Indo-European *gol(H)-wo- (“bald; bare, naked”), from *gelH- (“head; naked”); or * from Latin calvus (“bald”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *kl̥H- (“ba
s: Those three young men are particularly callow youths.

d: An event or situation that happens at the same time as or in connection with another
ety: First attested 1607; from Middle French concomitant, from Latin concomitāns, the present participle of concomitor (“to accompany”), from con- (“together”) + comitor (“to accompany”), from comes (“companion”).
s: A major concomitant of the advent of diesel traction has been a vast increase in the amount of electrical equipment needing overhaul.

d: Speak unfavorably about
ety: From Latin trādūcō (“carry over; lead as a spectacle, dishonor”), from trāns + dūcō (“to lead”). Doublet of transduce, from Latin trānsdūcō.
s: Someone must have traduced Joseph K., for without having done anything wrong he was arrested one fine morning.

d: Something that precedes and indicates the approach of something or someone
ety: Originally, a person sent in advance to arrange lodgings. From Middle English herberjour, herbergeour, from Old French herbergeor (French hébergeur), from herbergier (“to set up camp; to shelter; to take shelter”) + -or (suffix forming agent nouns), from Old High German heribergan, ultimately from Proto-West Germanic *harjabergu (“army camp, shelter”). Compare German Herberge, Italian albergo, Dut
s: I knew by these harbingers who were coming.

d: A pale and sickly appearance
ety: From French étiolé, past participle of étioler (“to blanch”).
s: His etiolation signaled years in prison.

d: Very light rain; stronger than mist but less than a shower
ety: From Late Middle English misellen (“to drizzle”), cognate with Low German miseln, musseln (“to mizzle”), Dutch miezelen (“to drizzle, rain gently”). Of obscure origin, possibly a frequentative related to the base of mist; or, related to Middle Low German mes (“urine”), Middle Dutch mes, mis (“urine”), both from Old Saxon mehs (“urine”), from Proto-Germanic *mihstuz, *mihstaz, *mihsk- (“urine”), fr
s: When a gawping Byzantine head bounced past his feet, and a mizzle of blood settled upon him, something changed.

d: Marked by quiet and caution and secrecy; taking pains to avoid being observed
ety: Borrowed from Latin surrēptīcius (“furtive, clandestine”), from surrēpō (“to creep along”).
s: He read the letter aloud. Sophia listened with the studied air of one for whom, even in these days, a title possessed some surreptitious allurement.

d: An engine that provided medieval artillery used during sieges; a heavy war engine for hurling large stones and other missiles
ety: From Old French trebuchet, trebuket et al. (modern trébuchet), from trebuchier (“to overthrow, topple”), from tres- + *buchier, from Old French buc (“trunk of the body”), from Old Frankish *būk (“belly, trunk, torso”), from Proto-Germanic *būkaz (“belly, abdomen, trunk”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰōw- (“to blow, swell”). Cognate with Old High German būh (“belly”), Old English būc (“belly, trunk”
s: Medieval trebuchets are said to have been capable of launching 90-kg projectiles over distances of more than 300 meters.

d: Impossible to measure or compare in value or size or excellence
ety: From Middle French incommensurable, from Medieval Latin incommensurabilis. Its full etymology is equivalent to that of in- + commensurable.
s: The side and diagonal of a square are incommensurable with each other; the diameter and circumference of a circle are incommensurable.

d: Attempting to win favor from influential people by flattery
ety: From Ancient Greek σῡκοφᾰντῐκός (sūkophăntĭkós). By surface analysis, sycophant + -ic.
s: The sycophantic slags all say / "I knew him first, and I knew him well"

d: A card game for two players using a reduced pack of 32 cards
ety: From French piquet.
s: They would kick off their shoes and play piquet by candle-light.

d: One who habitually ignores the law and does not answer court summonses
ety: From scoff + law. Coined simultaneously by Mr Henry Irving Dale and Miss Kate L. Butler for a contest held in Boston in 1923 in which a word for "a lawless drinker of illegally made or illegally obtained liquor" was sought during the Prohibition era.
s: Unrepentant scofflaw on the lam Layin' waste to all the best-laid plans

d: Cause to be confused emotionally
ety: From be- + muse. In meaning, influenced by bemaze and later amuse.
s: This old man generally bemused himself in beer, once a fortnight.

d: A windstorm that lifts up clouds of dust or sand
ety: Borrowed from Italian scirocco (“south-east wind”).
s: But come, the board is spread; our silver lamp / Is trimm’d, and heeds not the sirocco’s damp.

d: A (usually canopied) seat for riding on the back of a camel or elephant
ety: From Hindi हौदा (haudā), from Arabic هَوْدَج (hawdaj, “litter carried by a camel”) (1774).
s: They don't ask for palanquins and howdahs.

d: Bursting into flower
ety: From a- (“in”) + bloom (“flower”).
s: When they returned, Jade's cheeks were abloom, her eyes alight with anticipation.

d: A uniformed doorman
ety: Borrowed from French commissionaire, from Latin commissio. Doublet of commissioner.
s: When the day came Nick turned up early at the bank and waited under a palm tree in the atrium. People hurried in, nodding to the commissionaire, who still wore a tailcoat and a top hat.

d: Make clear and (more) comprehensible
ety: From Late Latin ēlūcidātus, perfect passive participle of ēlūcidō (“to lighten, enlighten”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from ē(x)- (“out, from”) + lūcidus (“bright, clear, understandable”) + -ō (first conjugation verb-forming suffix), literally “to make light of (something)”, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *lewk- (“bright; to see; to shine”). Compare French élucider.
s: Another appendix elucidates the S.E.C.R. headcode system.

d: A mythical monster having the head of man (with horns) and the body of a lion and the tail of a scorpion
ety: From Latin mantichōras, from Ancient Greek μαρτιχόρας (martikhóras, “man-eater; tiger”), from Old Persian *martyahvārah (“man-eater”), from 𐎶𐎼𐎫𐎡𐎹 (m-r-t-i-y /⁠martyaʰ⁠/, “man”).
s: Now may I present to you the basilisk? Please down your goggles if you wish to resist From the fiery depths of the planet’s core The never sleeping for want of eating unholy stench of the manticore

d: The ritual washing of a priest’s hands or of sacred vessels
ety: From Middle English ablucioun (“cleansing of impurities”), from Old French ablution, and its source, Late Latin ablūtiō (“a washing away”), from abluō (“wash away”), from ab- (“away”) + lavō (“wash”).
s: There are now indications that it has caused some Americans to become more spartan when it comes to ablutions.
